text: Every quantum state you'll represent in code, a qubit amplitude pair, a two-qubit vector, a gate matrix, is a grid of numbers that needs real math applied to it, not just storage. Python lists store numbers; NumPy arrays let you compute with them the way physics notation expects.

A Python list is a general-purpose container with no idea its contents are numbers, so its operators do container things, not math things. A NumPy array overloads those same operators to mean actual arithmetic, backed by a fixed data type and one contiguous block of memory, which is exactly what makes vectorized math both possible and fast. You still reach for a plain list for anything you're not doing arithmetic on, like file paths or labels.

Here's the core difference, side by side. On a list, a times 2 duplicates the whole list into eight elements. On a NumPy array holding the same four numbers, arr times 2 doubles every entry: two, four, six, eight. Same syntax, completely different operation.

This matters immediately for representing a qubit. state equals an array of 0.6 and 0.8, squared element-wise and summed with np dot sum, comes out to exactly 1.0, zero point three six plus zero point six four, confirming this is a validly normalized qubit where the total probability is exactly one.
Next lesson covers the small set of NumPy operations, the at-sign operator, transpose, and complex conjugate, that make up essentially all the matrix math in quantum computing code.
